items.title: Ponytail: I CAN'T GO BACK FROM THIS NOW! 3X BETTER & LOWER TOKENS!
items.summary:
Visit Verdent: https://www.verdent.ai/?id=700712
Visit AISeeKing (my second channel with more cool ai stuff): https://www.youtube.com/@aiseeking

In this video, I'll be telling you about Ponytail, a new AI agent skill that prevents coding agents from over-engineering simple tasks. It encourages agents to reuse existing code, choose native platform features, avoid unnecessary dependencies, and write only the minimum amount of safe, maintainable code.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Ponytail turns AI coding agents into “lazy senior developers” that prioritize simple, effective solutions.
🪜 Its decision ladder checks existing code, standard libraries, native features, and installed dependencies before adding new code.
✂️ Ponytail can reduce generated code by up to 94% on common over-engineering tasks.
💸 Benchmarks show fewer tokens, lower costs, and faster execution without compromising safety.
🤖 It supports Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Verdent, and many other AI coding tools

items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I'd like to tell you that I have become more active on my AIC King channel. Now, I am posting some new stuff and some developer related tools that I don't cover here. So, you can go ahead and check it out as well. I'll put the link to it in the description. So, today we're looking at a tool that fixes one of the most annoying things about AI coding agents, which is overengineering. You know exactly what I'm talking about. You ask the AI for a simple date picker and it installs a whole library, creates a wrapper component, adds a stylesheet, and then starts a philosophical discussion about time zone handling. All of that for something the browser can literally do natively in one line. Well, this new tool is called Ponytail, and it's made by Dietrich Gert. It's an AI agent skill or plugin that makes your agent behave like a lazy senior developer. And I mean lazy in the best possible way. The whole motto of the project is he says nothing, he writes one line, it works, which is just amazing. It's also blowing up on GitHub with over a 100,000 stars. So, people clearly want this. And after trying it out, I can see why. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about what Ponytail actually does. The core idea is that AI agents write way too much code by default. They love creating abstractions, adding config options nobody asked for, and installing dependencies for things that already exist in the standard library. Ponytail injects a set of minimalism rules into your agent so that before it writes any code, it walks through a decision ladder. The ladder goes like this. First, does this thing even need to exist? If not, skip it. That's the classic Yagny principle. Second, is it already in the codebase? Then reuse it. Don't rewrite it. Third, does the standard library provide it? Use that. Fourth, is there a native platform feature for it? Use that. Fifth, is there an already installed dependency that does it? Use that. Sixth, can it be done in one line? Then it's one line. And only after all of that fails does the agent get to write new code. And even then, only the minimum necessary. Now, here's the important part, and I really like that they made this explicit. The ladder runs after the agent understands the problem. So, it still reads the relevant code and traces the actual flow first. It's not just blindly deleting stuff or writing cryptic oneliners to look clever. And it never cuts corners on validation, error handling, security, or accessibility. The code is minimal because it's necessary, not because it's artificially compressed. So, this is great for sure. Let me give you their own example because it's honestly perfect. You ask for a date picker component without ponytail. The agent installs flatpicker, creates a wrapper component, adds a stylesheet, and starts discussing time zones. With ponytail, you get a single input element with the type set to date and a little comment above it saying ponytail browser has one. That's it. Chef's kiss. Really good stuff. Now, let's see how to set it up. If you're using claude code, it ships as a proper plugin. Just run /plugin marketplace ad followed by dietri/ ponytail, then run /plugin install ponytail at ponytail, and that's it. You're good to go. If you're on Codex, it's basically the same thing, but from the terminal, you run Codex plug-in marketplace, add Dietrich Eert/Ponytail, and then Codex plugin add Ponytail at Ponytail. And this is where it gets impressive because Ponytail supports around 20 different agents. GitHub Copilot CLI has it through the Copilot plug-in commands. Gemini CLI can install it with the Gemini extensions install command pointing at the repo. There's support for Hermes Agent, Devon, CLI, Grock, Build, OpenClaw, Coder, Open Code, and a bunch more. And even if your tool doesn't support plugins at all, there's an instruction mode. The repo ships ready-made rule files for basically everything. Cursor users copy the files from the cursor rules folder. Windsurf users get awinsurf rules folder. Client gets rules. Copilot chat gets a co-pilot instructions file. And for tools like ADER or Zed, you can just drop the agents.mmd file into your project route or home directory. And the rules are always on. So no matter what you're using, you're covered, which is pretty good for sure. One thing to note is that the plug-in versions use NodeJS life cycle hooks. So you'll need Node on your path for those. The hooks are what inject the active rule set before each turn, and they also inject the rules into any sub aents that get spawned, which is a really nice touch. If you're using the instructiononly files, you don't need node at all. Now, let's talk about the modes because this is where it gets fun. Ponytail has three intensity levels plus off. You control them with the / ponytail command followed by light, full, ultra, or off. Light is the gentle version of the rules. Full is the default balance mode. And honestly, this is what I'd recommend for most people. And then there's ultra, which the readme describes as being for when the code base has wronged you personally. I laughed at that one. Ultra is the aggressive minimalism mode where the agent goes full deletion machine. Take it easy with that one on production code. Beyond the mode switching, you get a few more commands. / ponytail review scans your current diff and flags overengineering with actual deletion suggestions. / ponytail audit does the same thing but for your entire repository so you can find all the architectural bloat that's accumulated over time. This one is honestly my favorite because running it on an older project is a humbling experience. Then there's / ponytail debt. So when ponytail defers an optimization and leaves one of those little ponytail comments in the code, this command collects all of them into an actionable ledger. That way minimalism today doesn't mean forgotten work tomorrow. There's also/ ponytail gain which shows you a scoreboard of the measured improvements and/ ponytail help for a quick reference. Just keep in mind that the commands only work on skill capable hosts. The instructiononly setups get the always on rules but no commands. Now let's come to the numbers because they actually benchmark this properly instead of just claiming it works. They ran a real clawed code agent through 12 feature tasks on the full stack fast API template repository once with ponytail and once without. The results are pretty wild. 54% fewer lines of code on average. And on the classic overengineering traps it got up to 94%. The date picker went from 404 lines to 23. The color picker went from 287 lines to 23. On top of that, tokens went down by around 22%. Cost went down by 20% and execution time dropped by 27%. And here's the part that actually matters. The safety rating stayed at 100%. So all the validation, security, and accessibility stuff was preserved while everything else got cut down. Less code, less cost, less time. same safety. This is pretty amazing to be honest. And if you think about it, this pays for itself immediately. If you're on a cloud code subscription and constantly hitting your limits, 22% fewer tokens is not a small thing. And fewer lines of code also means less code to review, less code to maintain, and fewer places for bugs to hide. The cheapest code is the code that was never written. By the way, even the license fits the theme. It's MIT, which they point out is intentionally the shortest workable license. The commitment to the bit is real. Now, before I give you my verdict, let me quickly show you how I'm running this in Verdant because it honestly fits in really nicely there. If you're new here, Verdant is an AI coding tool that I've covered quite a bit on the channel. The quick overview is that it's built around delegation instead of babysitting. You describe a task, an agent plans it, codes it, and verifies its own work. You can also spin up multiple agents in parallel, each in its own isolated workspace with git work trees so they don't step on each other. And on top of that, it has a proper rules system. You get global user rules through verdant.mmd, project rules through agents.mmd, plan rules, and custom sub aents. And that rules system is exactly why ponytail slots write in. Remember the instructionon mode I mentioned? Ponytail ships an agents.mmd file and Verdant reads exactly that. So the install is literally just dropping ponytails agents.mmd into your project route and every verdant agent touching that repo now follows the lazy senior dev rules. If you want it everywhere, put the rules into your verdant.mmd user rules instead and they're always on across all your projects. No hooks, no node, nothing to configure. And because the rules ride along into sub agents and parallel agents, too, even your side tasks stay minimal. It's honestly one of the cleanest pairings because Verdant handles the orchestration and Ponytail handles the restraint. So, so what's my verdict? I think this is one of those ideas that seems obvious in hindsight, but nobody packaged it properly until now. Every AI agent right now has a bias toward writing more code because more code looks like more work is getting done. But anyone who has maintained a real project knows the that the best pull requests are often the ones that are mostly read. Ponytail basically encodes that senior developer instinct into a set of rules and makes it portable across 20 different agents. If you ask me, the full mode is the sweet spot for daily use. And the / ponytail audit command alone is worth the install. It's free, it's open source, it takes about a minute to set up, and it'll probably save you money from day one. There's really no downside here. I like this a lot. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super [music] thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]
